summary: EarthScope – Trend Detective is an educational platform that turns real NASA Earth-observation data into a guided scientific investigation. Instead of simply displaying datasets or ready-made conclusions, EarthScope helps students move through the full research process: identifying an environmental variable, selecting a geographic region, forming a hypothesis, exploring a long-term time series, separating seasonal variation from long-term change, analyzing trends, testing statistical significance, and making an evidence-based conclusion. Our prototype uses real NASA datasets, including OMI/Aura NO₂ data for Greater Cairo from 2005–2025. In this case, Sen’s Slope estimates an increase of approximately 0.37 × 10¹⁵ molecules/cm² per decade, with a statistically significant Mann–Kendall p-value of 0.0017. EarthScope complements powerful NASA tools such as Giovanni, Worldview, and AppEEARS by adding an accessible educational investigation layer. Three students tested the prototype and independently reached the scientific conclusion. EarthScope connects authentic data, real analysis, and interactive learning to build practical scientific reasoning.
details:
What it does

EarthScope — Trend Detective is an interactive, game-style web application that teaches students and curious members of the public how to find out whether a change in the Earth system is real. NASA and its partners release decades of satellite data for free, yet a student who opens it faces a hard question: is the pattern I see a genuine long-term trend, or just natural variation? Seasonal cycles create waves that look like change, the same variable can rise in one region and fall in another, and proving a trend requires statistics most learners have never met.

EarthScope answers this with “cases”. Each case pairs a region with a variable from NASA data, and the student plays a scientific detective. Our featured case asks: is nitrogen dioxide (NO₂), an air pollutant, increasing over Greater Cairo? Instead of being handed the answer, the student must reach a conclusion from evidence.

How it works

The featured case uses monthly NO₂ observations from the Ozone Monitoring Instrument (OMI) on NASA’s Aura satellite (NASA/KNMI) for Greater Cairo, 2005–2025: 21 years. Our data team prepares and tests the analysis in advance, and the website reads the results from a structured data file.

The student then follows a seven-step investigation: a briefing with a plain-language definition of the variable; a hypothesis, locked in before any analysis (increase, decrease or no change); the raw time series with a period slider; a switch that removes the seasonal cycle by comparing each month with the long-term average of that same month, making the wave vanish and the true signal appear; the statistical test; a verdict (real trend, natural variation, or need more data) with a reason; and a final comparison between the student’s prediction and the scientific result.

We measure the rate of change with Sen’s slope and test significance with the Mann–Kendall test, shown with a 95% confidence interval and a p-value explained in plain words. For Greater Cairo, NO₂ rises about 0.37 × 10¹⁵ molecules/cm² per decade (roughly 7% of its mean level; 95% CI 0.17–0.63; p ≈ 0.0017): an increasing, statistically significant trend.

Benefits

EarthScope turns open NASA data from something students look at into something they can reason with. Predicting first exposes misconceptions; the seasonal switch makes the hardest concept visible in seconds; and the statistics are translated into plain language without hiding the method. Students learn the full scientific cycle (question, hypothesis, data, analysis, conclusion) and the habit of asking, “is this change real?” Teachers and self-learners get a ready-made guided activity that needs no software installation, only a browser. Because the design separates analysis from presentation, new regions and variables can be added simply by supplying new data. We also tested EarthScope with three students, who followed the journey and reached the conclusion without help.

Programming languages used

Python (data processing and statistical analysis: seasonal removal, Sen’s slope, Mann–Kendall test); JavaScript, HTML and CSS (the interactive website and charts).
